props.title: X2: X-Men United
props.initialSlug: Mutants unite against a deadly anti-mutant conspiracy

sections.content: X2: X-Men United turbocharged the superhero genre by diving deeper into mutant persecution and prejudice. Bryan Singer's sequel elevated the stakes from the first X-Men film by opening with Nightcrawler's breathtaking White House attack sequence - a technical marvel that holds up 20 years later. The film drew clear parallels to LGBTQ+ rights through Bobby "Iceman" Drake's coming out scene, continuing the X-Men's long tradition of addressing civil rights through the lens of mutant discrimination. This approach influenced later superhero films like Black Panther (2018) and Captain America: Civil War (2016) to tackle real-world issues head-on.

sections.content: X2's influence on superhero ensemble storytelling can't be overstated. The film juggled multiple character arcs - Wolverine's origin hunt, Jean Grey's growing powers, Stryker's anti-mutant crusade - while maintaining narrative cohesion. This blueprint laid groundwork for ambitious team-ups like The Avengers (2012) and Justice League (2017). The movie's practical effects and considered use of CGI created a grounded feel that later X-Men films struggled to maintain. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Impact

By positioning Colonel William Stryker as a human antagonist rather than a mutant threat, X2 complicated the franchise's good vs. evil dynamic. This nuanced approach to villainy influenced films like Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014) and Black Panther (2018) to explore antagonists with understandable - if misguided - motivations. The film's darker tone and political themes helped legitimize comic book movies as serious filmmaking, paving the way for acclaimed works like The Dark Knight (2008).
